lessons.title: Your First C# Program, and What the Compiler Is Doing
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## A compiled, statically typed language

C# is compiled before it runs and every variable has a type known at compile time. That sounds like bureaucracy when you come from a scripting language. It is not — it is a large class of bugs being caught while you type instead of in production.

When you write `int count = "seven";` the compiler refuses. That refusal is the feature.

## What actually happens when you run it

Your `.cs` files are compiled to an intermediate language (IL), which the .NET runtime turns into machine code as it executes. You do not need to think about this often, but it explains two things you will notice: why the first call to a method is slower than the rest, and why a `.dll` can be inspected to see what types it contains.

## The shape of a program

Modern C# lets you write top-level statements with no visible class. That is convenient for learning and fine for small tools. Real projects still organise code into namespaces and classes, because once there is more than one file you need somewhere to put things.

Start with top-level statements, and move to explicit classes the moment your file has more than one job.

## Variables, and why `var` is not dynamic

`var total = 10;` does not mean "untyped". The compiler infers `int` and it stays `int` forever. `var` saves typing, not type safety.

Use it when the type is obvious from the right-hand side, and write the type out when it is not.

## Strings are immutable

Every operation that looks like it changes a string actually makes a new one. `name += "x"` in a loop that runs ten thousand times creates ten thousand strings. That is the single most common accidental performance bug in beginner C#, and `StringBuilder` is the answer.
keyTakeaways: C# is compiled and statically typed; the compiler rejecting your code is the feature
Source becomes IL, which the runtime compiles as it executes
`var` is type inference, not dynamic typing — the type is fixed at compile time
Strings are immutable; building one in a loop allocates a new string each time

questions.prompt: What does `var` do in C#?
questions.explanation: `var` asks the compiler to infer the type from the initialiser. The variable is then statically typed for its whole life — nothing about it is dynamic.

options.text: Infers the type at compile time; the variable is statically typed thereafter
Makes the variable dynamically typed
Allows the variable to hold any type at runtime
Defers type checking until runtime

lessons.title: Value Types, Reference Types and Null
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Two kinds of variable

An `int`, a `bool`, a `DateTime` or a `struct` holds its value directly. Assigning one copies the value.

A `class` instance, an array or a string holds a *reference* to an object elsewhere in memory. Assigning one copies the reference, and both variables now point at the same object.

This distinction explains a large share of confusing beginner bugs: you changed something through one variable and another variable changed too, because there was only ever one object.

## What this means in practice

Pass a `List<string>` to a method and the method can add to your list. Pass an `int` and it cannot change your number. Neither behaviour is wrong; you just need to know which one you have.

If you want a method not to modify a collection you pass it, either pass a copy or accept a read-only interface.

## Null is a reference thing

Value types cannot be null unless you mark them nullable with `?`. Reference types could always be null, and dereferencing null is the most common runtime crash in .NET.

## Nullable reference types are worth turning on

Modern C# projects enable nullable reference types, and then `string` means "never null" while `string?` means "might be null". The compiler warns you when you dereference something that might be null without checking.

Turn it on in every new project. It moves an entire bug category from runtime to compile time, which is the same trade that made static typing worth it in the first place.

## Records give you value semantics for classes

A `record` is a reference type that compares by value. Two records with identical contents are equal, which is what you usually want for data. Use them for anything that is data rather than behaviour.

modules.title: Collections and LINQ
modules.summary: Choosing the right container, and expressing what you want instead of how to loop for it.

lessons.title: Arrays, Lists and Dictionaries — Choosing the Right One
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Three containers cover most work

- **Array** — fixed size, fastest, use when the count is known and will not change.
- **`List<T>`** — grows as you add, indexed access, the default choice.
- **`Dictionary<TKey, TValue>`** — lookup by key in roughly constant time.

The decision that matters most is the third one. If your code ever does "loop through a list to find the item with this id", and does it more than occasionally, you want a dictionary.

## Why the dictionary matters so much

Finding an item in a list means checking each element in turn. With 10 items that is invisible. With 10,000 items inside another loop over 10,000 items, it is a hundred million comparisons and your program appears to hang.

This is the single most common accidental performance disaster in application code, and switching to a dictionary usually turns it into a few milliseconds.

## Pick the interface you expose carefully

Return `IReadOnlyList<T>` when callers should not modify what you hand back. Accept `IEnumerable<T>` when you only need to iterate once. Being specific in what you accept and restrictive in what you return is free documentation.

## HashSet for membership

When the only question is "have I seen this?", `HashSet<T>` answers in constant time and refuses duplicates automatically.

## Beware iterating while modifying

Adding to or removing from a collection while a `foreach` is running over it throws. If you need to remove items, collect them first and remove afterwards, or iterate a copy.
keyTakeaways: Array for fixed size, List for the general case, Dictionary for lookup by key
Searching a list inside a loop is the classic accidental performance disaster
Accept `IEnumerable<T>`, return `IReadOnlyList<T>` — specific in, restrictive out
HashSet answers membership questions and refuses duplicates
Modifying a collection during `foreach` throws — collect then remove

lessons.title: LINQ: Querying Collections Without Loops
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Say what you want, not how to get it

LINQ replaces a loop, a condition and an accumulator with one readable expression. `Where` filters, `Select` transforms, `OrderBy` sorts, `GroupBy` groups, and `Sum`, `Count`, `Any` and `First` produce a result.

The gain is not brevity. It is that the resulting line says what you meant, so a reader does not have to reconstruct the intent from the mechanics.

## Deferred execution is the thing to understand

`Where` and `Select` do not run when you write them. They build a query that runs when you enumerate it — with `foreach`, `ToList()`, `Count()` or similar.

Two consequences catch people out. First, if the underlying data changes between defining and enumerating, you see the new data. Second, enumerating the same query twice does the work twice.

When you need the results more than once, call `ToList()` and keep them.

## `First` versus `FirstOrDefault`

`First` throws when nothing matches. `FirstOrDefault` returns null (or the default value). Choose deliberately: if a missing match is a bug, `First` is right and the exception is informative. If a missing match is normal, `FirstOrDefault` with a null check is right.

Calling `First` on a query that legitimately finds nothing is a common source of production exceptions.

## Any() rather than Count() > 0

`Any()` stops at the first match. `Count()` walks everything. On a list the difference is negligible; on a database query or a large sequence it is not.

## Keep it readable

LINQ can express almost anything, including things nobody should read. If a chain needs more than about four operations, give intermediate results names. A query you cannot explain out loud is worse than the loop it replaced.
keyTakeaways: LINQ expresses intent: `Where`, `Select`, `OrderBy`, `GroupBy` plus a terminal operation
Queries are deferred — they run on enumeration, and enumerating twice works twice
`First` throws on no match, `FirstOrDefault` returns null; pick deliberately
`Any()` short-circuits where `Count() > 0` walks the whole sequence
Break long chains into named steps; unreadable LINQ is worse than a loop

questions.prompt: What does `orders.Where(o => o.Total > 100)` do at the moment that line executes?
questions.explanation: LINQ operators are deferred. The predicate runs when the query is enumerated, not when it is defined.

options.text: When a missing match indicates a bug and you want the exception

lessons.title: Exceptions: Throwing, Catching and When Not To
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Exceptions are for the exceptional

An exception says "I cannot complete this and cannot sensibly continue". A user typing an invalid date is not exceptional — it is Tuesday. Validate and return a result. A database that has vanished mid-transaction is exceptional.

Using exceptions for ordinary control flow makes code slow and hides real failures in noise.

## Catch what you can handle

The commonest beginner mistake is catching everything and carrying on:

```csharp
try { DoWork(); } catch { }
```

This converts a visible failure into a silent wrong answer, which is strictly worse. If you cannot do something meaningful with an exception, let it propagate to something that can.

## Catch specifically

Catch `FileNotFoundException`, not `Exception`. The specific catch documents what you expected to go wrong and leaves everything else alone.

## Never lose the stack trace

`throw;` rethrows preserving where the error came from. `throw ex;` resets the stack trace to this line and destroys your best diagnostic. This distinction costs people hours of debugging.

## Finally, or better, using

Cleanup that must happen regardless goes in `finally`. For anything implementing `IDisposable` — files, connections, HTTP clients — `using` does it for you and is harder to get wrong.

## Fail with a useful message

An exception message is read by someone under pressure who does not have your context. Include the values involved: not "invalid input" but "renewal_date '19/09/2026' could not be parsed for customer CUST-0042; expected ISO 8601".
keyTakeaways: Exceptions are for conditions you cannot handle, not routine validation
An empty catch turns a visible failure into a silent wrong answer
Catch the specific exception you expected; let everything else propagate
`throw;` preserves the stack trace, `throw ex;` destroys it
Use `using` for anything disposable; put values in the exception message

lessons.title: async and await Without the Deadlocks
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## What async is actually for

`async`/`await` is about *not holding a thread while waiting*. When your code calls a database or an HTTP API, most of the elapsed time is spent waiting for someone else. Without async, a thread sits blocked doing nothing. With it, that thread is released to serve another request and resumes yours when the answer arrives.

On a web server this is the difference between handling a few hundred concurrent requests and a few thousand. It does not make any single operation faster.

## async all the way up

If a method awaits something, it is `async` and returns `Task` or `Task<T>`. Its caller awaits it, so the caller is async too, all the way to the framework entry point.

Do not break the chain by calling `.Result` or `.Wait()` on a task. In some contexts that deadlocks, and in all contexts it blocks the thread you were trying to free.

## Return Task, not void

`async void` cannot be awaited and its exceptions cannot be caught by the caller — they crash the process. The only legitimate use is an event handler. Everywhere else, return `Task`.

## Await in parallel when the work is independent

Awaiting two independent calls in sequence takes the sum of their durations. Start both, then await both, and it takes the longer of the two. `Task.WhenAll` does this.

Only do this when the calls genuinely do not depend on each other, and be careful about how many you start at once — a thousand simultaneous requests will be rate-limited.

## Pass the cancellation token

Accept a `CancellationToken` and pass it down. When the caller gives up — the user navigated away, the request timed out — the work stops instead of continuing to consume resources for an answer nobody will read.

sequenceDiagram participant R as Request participant T as Thread pool participant D as Database R->>T: handle request T->>D: await query Note over T: thread RELEASED
serves other requests D-->>T: result ready Note over T: a thread resumes the method T-->>R: response
keyTakeaways: async frees the thread while waiting on I/O; it does not make a single call faster
Async propagates up the call chain — never break it with `.Result` or `.Wait()`
Return `Task`, not `void`; `async void` exceptions crash the process
Use `Task.WhenAll` for independent work to pay the longest duration, not the sum
Accept and pass a CancellationToken so abandoned work actually stops

lessons.title: Classes, Interfaces and the Case for Each
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## A class bundles data with the behaviour that owns it

The useful question is not "what are the nouns in my problem" but "what invariants does this thing protect". A `BankAccount` class exists because something must guarantee the balance never goes negative. If a class protects nothing and has only properties, it is data — make it a record.

## An interface is a promise about capability

`ITaskStore` says: whoever implements this can save and load tasks. It says nothing about whether that is a file, a database or a dictionary in memory.

That separation buys two concrete things. You can test the code that uses the store without a file system. And you can change the storage later without touching the logic.

## Do not write an interface per class reflexively

The habit of giving every class an interface with the same name and an `I` in front produces twice the files and no benefit. Introduce an interface when there is a real reason: a second implementation, a test double, or a boundary you want to keep stable.

One implementation and no tests against it means you have written a second name for the same thing.

## Inheritance is the weakest of the options

`class Manager : Employee` couples them permanently, and the coupling is inherited by every future change. Composition — holding a reference to something and delegating — keeps the pieces independent.

Prefer interfaces for polymorphism and composition for reuse. Reach for inheritance when the subtype genuinely *is* the base type in every context, which is rarer than it first appears.

## Sealed by default is a reasonable habit

A class not designed to be inherited from should say so. It documents intent and prevents someone building on assumptions you never made.
keyTakeaways: A class earns its existence by protecting an invariant; pure data should be a record
An interface promises a capability and decouples users from implementations
Do not create an interface per class — require a second implementation or a test double
Prefer composition over inheritance; inheritance couples permanently
Seal classes you did not design for inheritance

lessons.title: Encapsulation and Making Invalid States Unrepresentable
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## The best validation is a type that cannot be wrong

Most defensive checks scattered through a codebase exist because some object could be constructed in a nonsensical state. Remove that possibility and the checks become unnecessary.

If an order must always have at least one line, do not create an empty order and validate later — require the lines in the constructor. Now "order with no lines" is not a bug to catch; it is a program that does not compile.

## Private setters and real constructors

A class with public setters on everything is a bag of fields. Anyone can put it into any state at any time, and no method can rely on anything.

Make the constructor establish a valid object, keep setters private, and expose deliberate methods for the transitions that are allowed. `order.Cancel()` can enforce that a shipped order cannot be cancelled; `order.Status = Cancelled` cannot.

## Enums over magic strings

A status that is a `string` accepts `"Compelte"`. A status that is an `enum` does not compile. This is the same principle applied to the smallest scale, and it is free.

## Expose collections read-only

A public `List<T>` property lets any caller add and remove items behind your back, bypassing every rule your class enforces. Expose `IReadOnlyList<T>` and provide explicit methods for the changes that are permitted.

## Guard at the boundary, trust inside

Validate input where it enters the system — the API, the file parser, the form. Once it is a domain object, the type guarantees hold and internal code does not need to re-check them.

The alternative, checking everywhere, is both slower and less reliable, because one forgotten check is a bug and nobody can tell which checks are still needed.
keyTakeaways: Prefer types that cannot represent an invalid state over validation after the fact
Establish validity in the constructor; keep setters private and expose intentional methods
Use enums instead of strings for fixed sets of values
Expose collections as read-only and provide explicit mutation methods
Validate at the boundary and trust the types inside

lessons.title: Dependency Injection: The Problem It Solves
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Start with the problem

A class that constructs its own dependencies is welded to them:

```csharp
public class TaskService
{
    private readonly JsonFileTaskStore _store = new("tasks.json");
}
```

You cannot test this without writing files. You cannot point it at a database without editing it. You cannot use two of them with different paths. The class decided something it had no business deciding.

## The fix is embarrassingly simple

Ask for the dependency instead of creating it:

```csharp
public class TaskService(ITaskStore store) { }
```

That is dependency injection. Everything else — containers, lifetimes, registration — is machinery for doing this at scale. The idea is just: take what you need as a parameter.

## What the container adds

In a real application, `TaskService` needs a store, which needs a connection, which needs configuration. Wiring that by hand at every call site is tedious and repetitive.

A container is told once how to build each thing, and constructs the whole graph on demand. ASP.NET Core has one built in, and you register services at startup.

## Lifetimes, briefly

- **Transient** — a new one every time. The safe default.
- **Scoped** — one per web request. Correct for anything holding request state, including a database context.
- **Singleton** — one for the application's lifetime. Fine for stateless helpers and configuration; dangerous for anything holding mutable state, because every request shares it.

The classic production bug is injecting a scoped database context into a singleton, which keeps one context alive forever.

## Depend on the interface

Take `ITaskStore`, not `JsonFileTaskStore`. Taking the concrete type gives up everything the injection was for.
keyTakeaways: A class that constructs its own dependencies cannot be tested or reconfigured
Dependency injection is simply taking what you need as a constructor parameter
A container builds the object graph so you do not wire it by hand everywhere
Transient by default, scoped for per-request state, singleton only when stateless
Inject a scoped context into a singleton and it lives forever — a classic production bug

lessons.title: Single Responsibility Without Ceremony
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## One reason to change

A class should have one reason to change. Not one method, not one line — one *reason*.

The practical test is whether you can describe what it does in a sentence without using "and". "Loads tasks from a file, formats them for display and sends the overdue ones by email" is three reasons, and a change to any one of them risks the other two.

## Notice the mixed levels

A method that opens a file, parses dates, applies a business rule and writes HTML is operating at four different levels of abstraction at once. That is the readable symptom of a responsibility problem, and it is easy to spot without invoking principles.

Good code reads at one level per method, with details delegated downward.

## Do not over-apply it

The common failure is the opposite: a codebase where every class has one method, nothing can be understood without opening nine files, and the indirection hides rather than reveals.

Split when a class has genuinely separate reasons to change, or when it has become hard to test. Do not split because a rule says small is good.

## Let the tests tell you

A class that needs six mocks to test is telling you something. So is one where half the tests set up state that the other half ignores.

Test difficulty is the most honest signal about structure available, and it arrives before the design problem becomes expensive.

## A pragmatic order

Write it as one thing. Get it working and tested. Split it when a second reason to change actually arrives, and let the tests guide where the seam goes.

Designing the seams in advance is how you end up with elaborate structure serving requirements that never materialised.
keyTakeaways: One class, one reason to change — test it by describing it without saying “and”
Mixed levels of abstraction in one method are the readable symptom
Over-splitting is as damaging as under-splitting; indirection can hide rather than reveal
Test difficulty is the earliest honest signal that a class does too much
Write it whole, then split when a second reason to change actually arrives

modules.title: Testing
modules.summary: Tests that catch regressions rather than restating the implementation.

lessons.title: Your First Unit Tests with xUnit
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## What a unit test is for

It pins behaviour down so that a future change that breaks it is noticed immediately, by a machine, rather than eventually, by a user.

That framing decides what to test. Test the behaviour someone depends on. Do not test that a property returns what you just set — that tests the compiler.

## Arrange, act, assert

Three parts, in order, with a blank line between them:

```csharp
var service = new TaskService(new InMemoryTaskStore());   // arrange
var task = await service.AddAsync("Write tests");         // act
Assert.Equal(TaskStatus.Open, task.Status);               // assert
```

When a test has two acts, it is two tests.

## Name the test as a sentence

`AddAsync_GivenBlankTitle_Throws` tells you what broke without opening the file. `Test1` does not. The name is read far more often than the body — usually in a CI failure list at an inconvenient moment.

## Theory for the same behaviour with different data

`[Fact]` is one case. `[Theory]` with `[InlineData]` runs the same test over several inputs, each reported separately, so you see exactly which input failed.

## Test the edges

The interesting cases are empty, one, many, null, boundary values and the failure path. The happy path with typical values is the case least likely to break.

## One assert per concept

Several asserts are fine if they check one behaviour. But when a test asserts six unrelated things, the first failure hides the rest and you fix them one run at a time.
keyTakeaways: A test pins behaviour so a machine catches the regression, not a user
Arrange, act, assert — two acts means two tests
Name tests as sentences; the name is read far more often than the body
Use `[Theory]` with `[InlineData]` so each input reports separately
Test empty, one, many, null, boundaries and failures — not the comfortable middle

questions.explanation: Each case is reported as its own test, so a failure names the exact input. A loop stops at the first failure and hides the rest.

options.text: Each input is reported separately, so you see exactly which one failed
Theories run faster than facts

lessons.title: Testing Code That Talks to the Outside World
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## The boundary is the problem

Code that reads files, calls HTTP APIs, queries databases or asks for the current time is awkward to test. Tests become slow, need infrastructure, and fail for reasons unrelated to your change.

The fix is not a clever mocking framework. It is putting those things behind an interface so a test can supply something else.

## Fakes usually beat mocks

A **fake** is a working implementation that is simpler — an in-memory store, for example. A **mock** is configured to expect particular calls and verify them.

Prefer fakes. A fake tests behaviour: put a task in, get it out. A mock often tests implementation: assert that `SaveAsync` was called exactly once. The second kind breaks when you refactor without changing behaviour, which teaches everyone to distrust the suite.

Use a mock when the interaction *is* the behaviour — "an email must be sent" is a legitimate thing to verify.

## Time is a dependency

`DateTime.Now` inside a method makes "what happens after the due date" untestable without waiting. Inject `TimeProvider` (built into modern .NET) and a test can state the date.

Anything non-deterministic deserves the same treatment: random numbers, new GUIDs, the machine name.

## Know which kind of test you are writing

A **unit test** exercises your logic with everything external faked. Milliseconds, run constantly.

An **integration test** exercises the real thing — a real database, the real HTTP pipeline. Slower, fewer, and the only way to catch the mistakes that live in the wiring.

You need both. Unit tests alone pass while the application fails to start.

## Do not fake what you own and can use directly

An in-memory SQLite database is often better than faking a repository: it tests your actual queries. Fake at the edges you genuinely cannot control — third-party APIs, the clock, the network.

flowchart TB
  subgraph Unit["Unit test — milliseconds, run constantly"]
    A[Your logic] --> B[Fake store]
    A --> C[Fake clock]
    A --> D[Fake email]
  end
  subgraph Integration["Integration test — slower, fewer"]
    E[Real HTTP pipeline] --> F[Real logic]
    F --> G[(In-memory database)]
  end

Prefer fakes over mocks: fakes test behaviour, mocks often test implementation
Inject `TimeProvider` rather than calling `DateTime.Now` inside logic
Unit tests for logic, integration tests for wiring — you need both
Fake only what you cannot control; a real in-memory database beats a fake repository

lessons.title: How a Request Becomes a Response in ASP.NET Core
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## A pipeline of middleware

A request arrives and passes through an ordered sequence of components. Each one can act on the request, pass it along, and act on the response coming back. Routing matches a URL to an endpoint; your handler runs; the response travels back out through the same components in reverse.

Almost every confusing ASP.NET Core problem is an ordering problem. Authentication placed after authorisation means nobody is ever authenticated. Exception handling placed late means early failures are not caught.

## Where your code sits

Your controller or minimal-API handler is at the end of the pipeline. By the time it runs, routing has matched, the body has been bound to your parameter, and authentication has established who is calling.

## Model binding, then validation

The framework reads the request body, query string and route values and populates your parameters. If JSON does not match the target type, binding fails before your code runs and the caller gets a 400.

Validation attributes are then checked, and in an API controller a failure is automatically turned into a 400 with the field details. You do not write that code.

## Minimal APIs or controllers

Minimal APIs declare endpoints as lambdas — less ceremony, good for small services. Controllers group related endpoints in a class — more structure, better when there are many.

Both use the same pipeline and the same binding. Pick one and be consistent; the choice matters far less than people argue.

## Keep handlers thin

A handler should bind input, call a service, and map the result to a response. Business logic in a controller cannot be tested without the web stack and cannot be reused by anything else.
lessons.diagramMermaid:
flowchart LR A[Request] --> B[Exception handler] B --> C[HTTPS redirect] C --> D[Authentication] D --> E[Authorization] E --> F[Routing + model binding] F --> G[Your handler] G --> H[Service] H --> G G --> I[Response back out
through the same layers]
keyTakeaways: A request passes through ordered middleware; most confusing bugs are ordering bugs
By the time your handler runs, routing, binding and authentication have happened
Binding failures produce a 400 before your code runs; validation attributes do the same
Minimal APIs and controllers share the pipeline — pick one and be consistent
Handlers bind, delegate and map; logic belongs in a service

lessons.title: Status Codes, Validation and Error Responses That Help
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## The status code is part of the contract

Callers branch on it. Returning 200 with `{"error": "not found"}` forces every client to parse the body to discover whether it worked, and most will not — they will treat it as success.

The ones that carry most of the load:

- **200 OK** — it worked.
- **201 Created** — a resource was created; include its location.
- **204 No Content** — it worked and there is nothing to return. Common for delete.
- **400 Bad Request** — the request itself is malformed or invalid.
- **401 / 403** — not authenticated / authenticated but not permitted. Different things.
- **404 Not Found** — the resource does not exist.
- **409 Conflict** — valid request, but it conflicts with current state. Borrowing a borrowed book.
- **422** — well-formed but semantically wrong. Optional; 400 is usually enough.
- **500** — you broke, not them. Never return this for a predictable case.

## 400 versus 409 is worth getting right

400 means "fix your request". 409 means "your request is fine, the world is not in the right state". A caller can retry a 409 later; retrying a 400 unchanged is pointless.

## Say which field is wrong

An error body naming the offending fields turns a support ticket into a self-service fix. ASP.NET Core produces this automatically from validation attributes, in the standard `ProblemDetails` shape.

## Never return exception details

Stack traces and connection strings in an error response are an information leak. Log the detail server-side with a correlation id, and return the id. Then "error 4f2a" lets you find everything in one query.

## Do not leak entities

Return a response model, not your EF entity. An entity carries navigation properties, database concerns and fields the caller should not see, and changing your database schema should not silently change your public API.
keyTakeaways: The status code is the contract; never signal failure with 200
400 means fix your request, 409 means the state conflicts — only one is retryable
Name the invalid fields; `ProblemDetails` is the standard shape
Never return exception detail; log it with a correlation id and return the id
Return response models, not EF entities — schema changes must not alter the public API

questions.prompt: A caller asks to borrow a book that exists but is already on loan. Which status code is correct?
questions.explanation: The request is valid; the current state conflicts with it. That is 409, and unlike a 400 it is meaningfully retryable later.

options.text: 409 Conflict
400 Bad Request
404 Not Found
200 OK with an error message in the body

questions.explanation: An entity exposes navigation properties and internal fields, and couples your public API to your database schema so a migration silently changes the contract.

options.text: It keeps internal fields hidden and stops schema changes silently altering the public API
Entities cannot be serialised to JSON

lessons.title: Mapping Your Model to Tables with EF Core
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## What an ORM is doing

EF Core translates your C# classes into tables, your LINQ into SQL, and the rows back into objects. It also tracks what you changed so `SaveChanges` can work out the right `UPDATE` statements.

Useful to know: it is not magic, and the SQL it generates is inspectable. Anyone who cannot see the SQL their ORM is producing will eventually be surprised by it.

## DbContext is your unit of work

A `DbContext` represents one conversation with the database. Register it as scoped so each web request gets its own, and never share one across threads — it is not thread-safe, and the resulting errors are confusing.

## Configure explicitly

Conventions get you started, but the important constraints should be stated: required fields, maximum lengths, decimal precision, unique indexes, delete behaviour.

Two that matter especially. **Decimal precision**: money defaulting to a low-precision column silently rounds. **Delete behaviour**: cascade delete is the default for required relationships, and can remove far more than you intended.

## Migrations are your schema history

`dotnet ef migrations add` generates a versioned change script; `dotnet ef database update` applies it. Commit migrations with the code that needs them, so any checkout can build the database from scratch.

Review the generated SQL before applying it to anything real. EF occasionally produces a destructive step — dropping and recreating a column — where you expected an alter.

## Never call EnsureCreated in production

It creates the schema once and then does nothing forever, so your first schema change silently fails to apply. Use migrations.
keyTakeaways: EF Core maps classes to tables and LINQ to SQL; always be able to see the SQL
DbContext is a unit of work — scoped per request, never shared across threads
State required fields, lengths, decimal precision, indexes and delete behaviour explicitly
Commit migrations with the code; review the generated SQL before applying it
`EnsureCreated` never applies later changes — use migrations

questions.explanation: It creates the schema once if it is absent and then does nothing. Every later model change silently fails to reach an existing database.

options.text: It creates the schema once and never applies later changes
It is slower than migrations
It only works with SQLite
It drops existing tables on every start

questions.explanation: Left to a provider default, the column may hold fewer decimal places than the value requires and round silently — typically discovered during an audit.

options.text: A default precision can silently round monetary values
Decimals are not supported without explicit configuration
It makes queries measurably faster

lessons.title: Querying Efficiently, and the N+1 Trap
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## The N+1 problem

You fetch 100 loans. Then, rendering each one, you touch `loan.Book.Title`. If `Book` was not loaded, EF issues a query for it — once per loan. One query became 101, and the endpoint that was fast with test data crawls in production.

This is the single most common performance defect in ORM code.

## Eager loading fixes it

`Include` tells EF to fetch the related data as part of the original query. One round trip instead of a hundred and one.

Be selective: `Include` everything and you pull large object graphs you do not need. Include what you will actually touch.

## Project instead, when you can

Better still, select only the columns you need with `Select`. EF translates this into a SQL projection, so the database returns four columns rather than whole rows with all their text fields.

This is usually the biggest single win available, and it removes the N+1 question entirely because there is nothing lazy left to load.

## AsNoTracking for reads

By default EF tracks every entity it returns so it can detect changes. For a read-only query that is pure overhead — memory and time spent watching objects nobody will modify.

Add `AsNoTracking()` to every query whose results you will not save. On list endpoints the difference is easily measurable.

## Do the filtering in the database

`ToList()` then `Where()` downloads the whole table and filters in memory. `Where()` then `ToList()` filters in SQL. The line that materialises is the line where the query runs, and everything after it happens on your server.

## Look at the SQL

Log generated SQL in development. Almost every ORM performance surprise is visible the moment you look, and invisible until you do.
lessons.diagramMermaid:
flowchart TB subgraph Bad["N+1 — 101 round trips"] A[SELECT loans] --> B[SELECT book WHERE id=1] A --> C[SELECT book WHERE id=2] A --> D[... 98 more] end subgraph Good["Projection — 1 round trip"] E["SELECT l.Id, b.Title, m.Name, l.DueOn
FROM Loans l JOIN Books b JOIN Members m"] end
keyTakeaways: N+1: touching a navigation property per row issues one query per row
`Include` eagerly loads related data in a single round trip — but only what you need
Projecting with `Select` returns only the required columns and removes N+1 entirely
`AsNoTracking()` on read-only queries avoids change-tracking overhead
Filter before materialising; log the generated SQL in development

questions.explanation: Each row's navigation property is resolved with its own query when it was not loaded up front, turning one query into one per row plus the original.

options.text: Change tracking is wasted work when nothing will be saved
It prevents other users from modifying the rows

lessons.title: Configuration, Secrets and Logging
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Configuration comes from layers

`appsettings.json`, then `appsettings.{Environment}.json`, then environment variables, then command-line arguments — each overriding the last. This is what lets one build run in three environments without recompiling.

## Never commit a secret

Connection strings with passwords, API keys and certificates do not belong in `appsettings.json`, because that file is in Git and Git remembers forever. A key committed and then removed is still a leaked key.

In development use `dotnet user-secrets`, which stores values outside the repository. In production use environment variables or the platform's secret store.

## Bind to typed options

Reading `Configuration["Storage:Path"]` scatters string keys through the codebase and fails at runtime when one is wrong. Binding a section to a class gives you compile-time names, and validation on startup turns a misconfigured deployment into an immediate, clear failure rather than a mysterious null two hours later.

## Structured logging

`log.LogInformation("Borrowed book {BookId} for member {MemberId}", bookId, memberId)` keeps the values as searchable fields, not just text. You can then query for every event with a given book id, which string-interpolated logs do not allow.

Use the message template with placeholders — never interpolate the values into the string yourself.

## Log levels mean something

**Information** for events worth knowing about in production. **Warning** for something recoverable that a human should eventually see. **Error** for a failed operation. **Debug** for development detail.

Logging everything at Information produces a volume nobody reads, which is the same as no logging.

## Never log secrets or personal data

Passwords, tokens, full card numbers and personal details must not reach the log. Logs are widely readable, retained for a long time and frequently exported.
keyTakeaways: Configuration layers: appsettings, environment file, environment variables, command line
Never commit secrets — use user-secrets in development and a secret store in production
Bind configuration to typed options and validate at startup
Use structured logging templates so values stay searchable fields
Match the level to the audience, and never log secrets or personal data

questions.prompt: Why use `log.LogInformation("Borrowed {BookId}", id)` rather than interpolating the id into the string?
questions.explanation: The template keeps BookId as a structured field, so logs can be queried by it. An interpolated string is only text and must be grepped.

options.text: The value stays a searchable structured field rather than becoming plain text
Interpolation does not compile inside logging calls
Templates produce shorter log lines

questions.prompt: A connection string with a password was committed to appsettings.json and removed in the next commit. What is the situation?
questions.explanation: Git retains history. The credential is still recoverable from the repository and must be rotated, not merely deleted.

options.text: The credential is still in Git history and must be rotated
Removing it in a later commit is sufficient
It is safe as long as the repository is private
Only a force-push is needed to make it safe

lessons.title: Integration Tests Over the Real Pipeline
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## What unit tests cannot catch

Unit tests exercise your logic with everything external replaced. That leaves a whole category untested: routing that does not match, a service that is not registered, middleware in the wrong order, a JSON property name the client does not expect, a migration that has not been applied.

Every one of those passes a full unit test suite and fails on first contact with a real request.

## WebApplicationFactory starts the real thing

It boots your application in memory, with the real pipeline, the real dependency injection and the real routing, and gives you an `HttpClient` that talks to it without a network port.

Tests then make real HTTP requests and assert on real responses — including the status code, which is the part a unit test never sees.

## Swap only what you must

Replace the database with something test-friendly and leave everything else alone. The more you substitute, the less you are testing.

An in-memory SQLite connection is a good choice: it is a real relational database, so constraints and your actual SQL are exercised, but it is created and discarded per test.

## Test the contract, not the internals

Assert on status codes, response shape and the effect on state. Do not assert on which internal method ran — that is what unit tests are for, and it makes the integration test brittle.

## Cover the failure paths

The 404 and the 409 are more likely to be wrong than the 200, because nobody exercises them by hand. They are also the paths clients depend on to behave correctly.

## A few, not hundreds

Integration tests are slower. A handful covering the important journeys, plus thorough unit tests underneath, is the right shape. Hundreds of integration tests produce a suite nobody waits for.
keyTakeaways: Unit tests cannot catch routing, registration, middleware order or serialisation mistakes
`WebApplicationFactory` boots the real pipeline in memory with a working HttpClient
Substitute only the database; the more you replace, the less you test
Assert on status codes, response shape and state — not on internal calls
Cover 404 and 409 especially, and keep the suite small enough that people run it

questions.explanation: Routing, service registration, middleware order and serialisation live in the wiring. Unit tests replace all of it, so they cannot see any of it.

Incorrect business rules

The database is the only replaceable service
